page.title: Virtual event platforms comparison guide
page.description: Compare virtual event platforms with checklists, cost models, staffing needs and a table to pick the right tool for webinars, summits or hybrid conferences.
page.h1: How do you compare virtual event platforms?
page.definition: A virtual event platform is software that hosts live or recorded online gatherings, handling streaming, registration, audience interaction and analytics for webinars, summits and hybrid conferences. It also provides branding tools, breakout rooms, networking features and integration with marketing automation so organizers can manage the full attendee lifecycle from invite to follow‑up.
page.quick_answer: Start by listing required capacity, interaction features and budget model, then match those needs to a shortlist of platforms using the comparison table below. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations.

sections.h2: What capacity and interaction features should I require?

blocks.p: Identify the maximum concurrent attendees, needed interaction tools and branding flexibility before shortlisting platforms. Match each requirement to the platform tier that supports it, because entry‑level plans often limit polls, breakout rooms or custom domains.

sections.h2: Which cost model fits my event type?

blocks.p: Choose a pricing structure that aligns with how often you host events and how many seats you need. Three common models exist: a per‑host licence sized by attendee capacity, a self‑serve monthly plan, and an annual contract negotiated with sales.

sections.h2: How many staff roles are needed for a webinar versus a summit?

blocks.p: A simple webinar can run with one producer while a summit demands a show caller, speaker manager, moderator and platform operator. Assign each role a clear owner to avoid gaps during live delivery.

sections.h2: What production steps must be completed before going live?

blocks.p: Complete a full rehearsal on the actual platform two to five days before the event and a technical check sixty minutes before start. Follow a run‑of‑show checklist to confirm slides, lower thirds, backup stream and moderator cues.

sections.h2: How do I evaluate platform reliability and support?

blocks.p: Test uptime history, support response times and data export capabilities before committing. Run a trial event and measure latency, failover behavior and the availability of a dedicated success manager.

ul: Live chat or phone support during events
Customer references from similar event sizes

faq.q: How long does it take to set up a virtual summit on a new platform?
faq.a: A summit typically requires six to eight weeks of planning, including platform configuration, speaker onboarding, run‑of‑show creation and a full rehearsal. A repeat format can move faster, but the first run needs the full timeline to avoid last‑minute gaps and ensure all integrations work.

faq.q: What is the difference between a platform licence and production services?
faq.a: A platform licence gives you software access for streaming, registration and analytics. Production services supply the crew, cameras, encoder, run‑of‑show management and backup stream. You purchase both separately; the platform does not include live direction or technical crew for the event.

faq.q: When should I send the event replay to attendees?
faq.a: Send the replay within twenty four to forty eight hours after the live session while the content is still fresh. Prompt delivery increases on‑demand views and gives sales teams a timely follow‑up asset and helps nurture leads for future events.

faq.q: Can I run a hybrid conference on a self‑serve platform?
faq.a: Self‑serve platforms can host the virtual portion of a hybrid conference, but venue AV, on‑site streaming hardware and a dedicated platform operator are still required. Plan the hybrid event six to eight weeks out and lock both venue and platform before finalising the agenda.
